We built a voice agent that hangs up on the "send me more info" excuse. It pulls the product up on your screen and starts driving it. Mid-call. By voice. This weekend at YC's Voice Agents Hackathon, hosted by Cekura & Daily , with NVIDIA , Amazon Web Services (AWS) , and Twilio , the rule was simple. No toy demos. Build a voice agent that survives production. So me and Nathan Yan built Pantheon. An entire outbound sales team in a box. Automated sales don't die on the pitch. They die because the customer doesn't truly get a personalized experience. We killed that. You type one line about what you sell. The agent finds a real decision maker, calls them, opens warm, handles objections, and then does the part that made people stop at our table: It texts them a link and co-browses a live product site WITH them in real time. "Show me an AC unit that can cool a 3000 sqft house and explain the costs and features." The store jumps to it. On their screen. While it's still talking. Interestingly, every call is also a test. Cekura throws simulated buyers at the agent and a self improvement loop rewrites its own playbook to close harder. The catch: it's forbidden from touching a single safety guardrail to do it. Avg Close rate: 45% to 73%, Made up facts: 0 It taught itself to close better while staying honest. That gap between an agent that demos pretty and one you'd actually trust to call your customers is getting slimmer by the day. Stack: Pipecat, NVIDIA Nemotron-3-Super, Twilio, Aviato, Cekura, FastAPI. Honest question: what's the first part of your sales process you'd actually hand to an agent? (Repo + 60 second demo, Watch the screen move. 👇) https://lnkd.in/gzvK66iz https://lnkd.in/gHZ3uksK #YCombinator #Hackathon ...more

Amazing competing and building at the Code and Capital Hackathon. I spent the weekend working on MedSim, a medical robotics simulation platform focused on generating synthetic 3D training data for high-risk surgical and robotics scenarios. The idea is that some of the most valuable robotics data is also the hardest to collect in the real world: rare events, unsafe failures, edge cases, tool interactions, and complex surgical environments. MedSim is designed to go beyond just rendering a 3D scene. The system focuses on structured scenario configs, simulation runs, event traces, replay validation, and outcome metrics so the generated data can support model training and evaluation. Huge thank you to the judges for the feedback and technical questions: Felipe Levi Gurgel , Enzo Cavalie , James Norman , and Ashtan Jordan . Thank you as well to the speakers, Michelle Shocron and Albert Hu, PhD , and to the mentors who shared their time and insights: Temi O. , Ryan D. Taylor , Indrajit Rajtilak , and Diana Munoz Lar . And thank you to the Code & Capital team, organizers, sponsors, and everyone I met throughout the weekend. It was a great environment to build, pitch, learn, and get real feedback. Excited to keep pushing MedSim forward. ...more

Last weekend, I had the opportunity to attend the Stanford LLM x Law Hackathon at Stanford Law School. Our team, Bridge, ended up placing 3rd, which I’m really grateful for. The event brought together 74 teams and over 600 participants, and it was a great environment to build in. I came in without a team, but that changed quickly when Ayomide "Ayo" Oloyede reached out and invited me to join. I’m glad it did, because it gave me the chance to work with him, Iris Cai , Malti John , and Tejaswita Kharel . Together, we built Bridge, a tool that helps junior lawyers learn from senior lawyers’ edits by turning redlines and revisions into structured, reusable guidance. What made the experience especially meaningful was how cross-functional it was. We were constantly thinking through the legal side, the technical side, and the product side at the same time, while trying to build something that would actually be useful in practice. In a short timeframe, that kind of environment forces clarity and good teamwork very quickly. I’m also really appreciative of all the conversations, feedback, and guidance throughout the event. Huge thanks to CodeX, The Stanford Center for Legal Informatics for organizing both the hackathon and especially to Jay Mandal , Roland Vogl , and Aparna Sinha for putting together such a thoughtful experience. I’m also grateful to the mentors from bayshore AI GmbH , Eudia , Filevine , and Harvey for their guidance. Overall, it was a really rewarding experience and a great reminder of how much meaningful work is happening at the intersection of law and AI. #AI #Law #Hackathon #AgenticAI #Startups ...more

Revenue went to $0 mid-fundraise. + Spent 6 months in an accelerator without finding an idea. Got held back a class. + 110+ investors passed on our pre-seed. It took 150 meetings to scrape together $500k. + Our next round had $500k committed. Our biggest investor backed out last-minute. We closed $250k and had to rescind a job offer. + Our biggest customer went bankrupt in 2023. + And many more. Today we have tens of millions in ARR, ~100-strong team in NYC, and help tens of thousands of salespeople every day. Rejection is inevitable when you’re doing hard things. The road to success is paved with failure.
